Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine

Vladimir Putin has once again set out his terms for ending the war in Ukraine, and once again they amount to a demand for capitulation rather than a basis for negotiation. Speaking to a room of officials in Moscow, the Russian president described the conditions as generous, while making clear that none of them had changed in any meaningful way since the talks began.

For Kyiv, the speech confirmed what its officials have said privately for months: the Kremlin is not negotiating over territory it claims to have annexed, it is simply waiting for the West to tire of the cost of supporting Ukraine. That reading is shared by several European diplomats who listened to the address and who described the language as deliberately uncompromising.

What made this speech different was not the substance but the timing. It came hours before a scheduled meeting of defence ministers, and a day after Washington repeated its call for both sides to come to the table without preconditions. The Russian leader did not mention that call at all, and instead repeated his claim that the war was forced upon him.

Analysts in Moscow say the message was aimed as much at domestic audiences as at foreign capitals. The Russian economy is absorbing the costs of the war better than many predicted, but the labour shortage and the interest rate are beginning to bite, and the president needed to project confidence rather than flexibility.

For the families of prisoners of war, the speech offered nothing new either. The exchange of captives continues at a slow pace, mediated by third countries, and every round is followed by the same public statements from both sides. Neither government has published a full list of those still held.

What happens next depends less on Moscow than on the capitals that supply Ukraine with weapons and money. The coming weeks will show whether the pressure that produced previous rounds of talks can be repeated, and whether either side is prepared to accept a ceasefire that does not settle the question of territory.
